mappings.note: How 'India' passed from Persian through Greek and Latin into international use - wholly a question of names taken up outside India, so LO-98.
Ancient Tamil verse on a king's domain from Cape Kumari to the northern mountains: content of a literary work of the time (LO-86) describing the land's extent (LO-82).
Why insiders and outsiders name a place differently - the item compares indigenous naming (LO-86) with foreign adaptation (LO-98), and needs both to answer.
The Indus as the root of Hind, Indoi and India; the naming chain (LO-98) hung on one physical feature (LO-82).
Traces Bharata and Jambudvipa through TEXTUAL evidence (LO-86, Mahabharata and Vishnu Purana) and INSCRIPTIONAL evidence (LO-89, Ashoka's edicts). The stem asks for both kinds by name.
The step-by-step reshaping of Sindhu in Persian, Greek and Chinese mouths - the fullest statement of the foreign-transmission theme, so LO-98 alone.
Sets Sapta Sindhava, Jambudvipa and Bharatavarsha against the different extents each covered - a synthesis across the chapter (LO-90) grounded in the texts that carry those names (LO-86).
How the Constitution settles the question of the country's name and why that mattered; a Constitution item, so CG-SST3, whose outcomes on diversity and local government do not reach it.
How a traveller's purpose - trade, pilgrimage, learning or conquest - coloured the name he gave the land. Every strand is a contact with a region outside India.
The Himalayas as the northern wall (LO-82) and the encircling oceans (LO-80) defining the subcontinent. The two features sit under different outcomes, so both are cited.
Compares Persian-derived Hindustan (LO-98) with Vedic and epic Bharata (LO-86) on etymology and usage - the comparison is the whole item.
How a language's missing sounds reshaped the borrowed name, Greek dropping the h of Hindu. Purely about transmission outside India, hence LO-98.
Justifies ancient Indian geographical knowledge from the Mahabharata's region lists, the Vishnu Purana's limits and Tamil poetry (LO-86), all describing India's extent (LO-82).
What 'heavenly master' reveals about Chinese regard for India as the home of Buddhism - the religion field of LO-98, at long-answer length.
Why ancient 'Hindu' must be read as a place name and not a faith; a caution about interpreting a foreign term, so LO-98.
Infers interaction across the subcontinent from the spread of regions the Mahabharata names (LO-86); drawing that inference from the map is the synthesis of LO-90.
Trade-route case: Persian 'Hidu' and Greek 'Indoi' for goods from a land of a mighty river - foreign naming and indirect Greek knowledge (LO-98) anchored on the Indus (LO-82).
Identifies Ashoka from a 250 BCE description of Jambudvipa and reads its political structure - the Mauryan inscriptional evidence of LO-89 with the textual name of LO-86.
Case turning on Article 1 and what choosing 'Bharat' on an official form signifies - a Constitution question throughout, so CG-SST3 with the other two.
Xuanzang's route, the Chinese names he would have known, his purpose and the reverence behind Tianzhu: a single sustained item on China's contact with India, so LO-98.
